The calculations on pristine and Fe-decorated BPN reveal pronounced anisotropy in the conductivity, with the value along one direction being significantly higher than that along the other. At 300 K, the overall conductivity is on the order of 10^5 S/m.

AI.tldr: This study systematically investigates Fe atom adsorption on monolayer and bilayer biphenylene network (BPN), showing that Fe adsorption enhances with coverage (optimal at 50% Fe/C ratio for monolayer), prefers interlayer four-membered ring centers in bilayer BPN (-4.3 eV), minimally affects in-plane mechanical properties, but dramatically boosts out-of-plane stiffness (C33 from 24.59 to 515.63 GPa at 25% Fe/C ratio), while conductivity exhibits strong anisotropy on the order of 10^5 S/m.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate the adsorption characteristics of Fe atoms on monolayer and bilayer biphenylene network (BPN), a 2D carbon allotrope, and evaluate how Fe decoration affects its mechanical and electronic properties.
AI.method: Structural optimization and adsorption energy analysis of Fe atoms on monolayer and bilayer BPN using computational methods; mechanical property evaluation (Young's modulus, shear modulus, out-of-plane elastic constant C33); electrical conductivity calculations.
AI.result: (1) Monolayer BPN: Fe adsorption strengthens with coverage, most stable at 50% Fe/C ratio. (2) Bilayer BPN: preferred Fe adsorption at interlayer four-membered ring center (-4.3 eV). (3) In-plane mechanical properties are largely unaffected by Fe adsorption. (4) Out-of-plane C33 of bilayer BPN dramatically increases from 24.59 GPa to 515.63 GPa at 25% Fe/C ratio. (5) Conductivity shows pronounced anisotropy, ~10^5 S/m at 300 K.
AI.conclusion: Fe decoration can significantly enhance the out-of-plane mechanical rigidity of bilayer BPN while preserving its in-plane stiffness, revealing tunable mechanical anisotropy; the material exhibits anisotropic conductivity suitable for electronic applications.

title: Competing incommensurability, electronic correlations, and superconductivity in a hybrid transition metal dichalcogenide
summary: The engineering of superlattices in two-dimensional van der Waals materials has enabled the realization of rich phase diagrams hosting topological and strongly correlated phases. While incommensurability is widespread in three-dimensional systems, the role of moiré potentials in bulk materials remains largely unexplored. Here, using scanning tunneling microscopy, we demonstrate that a bulk transition-metal dichalcogenide polytype, 4Hb-TaS$_2$, hosts an emergent incommensurate potential between its alternating 1T and 1H layers. Interplay with a concomitant incommensurate charge-density wave suppresses the long-range order of this potential, leading to intricate coupling with electronic correlations in the doped 1T surface layer. Combining density functional theory with dynamical mean-field theory, we show that the lattice mismatch locally modulates the interlayer distance, thereby tuning both hybridization and charge transfer between the correlated 1T and metallic 1H layers. This redistribution of charge drives the system towards a doped Mott regime, in which the remaining local moments become self-screened, giving rise to a zero-bias resonance. We further find that bulk superconductivity competes with both the underlying landscape and the associated charge transfer. Our results establish incommensurate potentials as a previously overlooked ingredient in hybrid transition-metal dichalcogenides, highlighting their central role in the interplay between electronic correlations, charge-density-wave order, and unconventional superconductivity.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that 4Hb-TaS₂, a bulk transition-metal dichalcogenide polytype, hosts an emergent incommensurate moiré potential due to lattice mismatch between its alternating 1T and 1H layers. Using STM and DFT+DMFT, the authors show this potential modulates interlayer distance, hybridization, and charge transfer, driving the doped 1T layer toward a self-screened doped Mott regime with zero-bias resonance, while bulk superconductivity competes with this landscape.
AI.motivation: While moiré potentials from lattice mismatch are well-explored in engineered 2D van der Waals superlattices, their role in bulk materials remains largely unknown. The authors aim to uncover whether incommensurate potentials exist in bulk crystals and how they influence electronic correlations, charge-density-wave order, and unconventional superconductivity.
AI.method: Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to observe the emergent incommensurate potential in bulk 4Hb-TaS₂; density functional theory combined with dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT) to model the effects of lattice mismatch on interlayer distance, hybridization, and charge transfer between correlated 1T and metallic 1H layers.
AI.result: The incommensurate potential from alternating 1T and 1H layers coexists with a charge-density wave that suppresses its long-range order. Lattice mismatch locally modulates interlayer distance, tuning hybridization and charge transfer. This charge redistribution drives the system toward a doped Mott regime where local moments become self-screened, producing a zero-bias resonance. Bulk superconductivity competes with both the incommensurate landscape and associated charge transfer.
AI.conclusion: Incommensurate potentials are a previously overlooked but central ingredient in hybrid TMDs, playing a key role in the interplay between electronic correlations, charge-density-wave order, and unconventional superconductivity in bulk materials.

title: Quantum-metric Bloch oscillations in weakly inhomogeneous electric fields
summary: Geometric analogs of Bloch oscillations studied so far have relied on Berry curvature. We show that a weakly inhomogeneous electric field adds a distinct quantum-metric term to semiclassical wavepacket dynamics, generating an oscillatory real-space contribution even when the Berry curvature vanishes. The associated transport response comprises an intrinsic and a scattering-time-dependent part. In the regime studied, the latter can dominate and approach finite saturation at high field when the relative field inhomogeneity is held fixed. A tilted Dirac model illustrates the mechanism. Realistic platforms will likely require synthetically engineered superlattices, with a finite quantum metric and an adequate band gap.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a weakly inhomogeneous electric field adds a quantum-metric term to semiclassical wavepacket dynamics, producing oscillatory real-space motion even without Berry curvature, with transport responses comprising intrinsic and scattering-time-dependent parts.
AI.motivation: Previous studies of geometric analogs of Bloch oscillations relied solely on Berry curvature; this work extends the understanding to systems where Berry curvature vanishes but quantum metric is present.
AI.method: The authors incorporate a weakly inhomogeneous electric field into semiclassical wavepacket dynamics and demonstrate the emergence of a quantum-metric contribution. A tilted Dirac model is used for illustration.
AI.result: The quantum-metric term generates oscillatory real-space dynamics even with zero Berry curvature. The transport response has an intrinsic part and a scattering-time-dependent part; the latter can dominate and saturate at high fields when relative field inhomogeneity is fixed.
AI.conclusion: Realistic platforms likely require synthetically engineered superlattices possessing finite quantum metric and adequate band gap.

title: Revisiting the high-field phase diagram of the topological cubic helimagnet SrFeO$_{3}$
summary: The cubic perovskite SrFeO$_{3}$ is a prototypical centrosymmetric itinerant magnet that hosts a quadruple-${\mathbf Q}$ hedgehog-antihedgehog lattice and exhibits a complex magnetic-field-temperature phase diagram. Yet, the microscopic mechanism underlying the emergence of its versatile multiple-${\mathbf Q}$ phases remains unresolved. Here, we elucidate the field-orientation dependence of the magnetic phase diagram and establish an effective spin Hamiltonian for SrFeO$_{3}$ that incorporates a cubic single-ion anisotropy together with bilinear and biquadratic interactions in momentum space. In addition, we observe magnetoelastic signatures of a first-order valence transition upon entering the forced FM phase at 40 T, which would be attributed to the suppression of negative charge transfer. These findings emphasize the pivotal importance of electronic itinerancy arising from the formation of a ligand-hole band in stabilizing multiple-${\mathbf Q}$ phases.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates SrFeO₃, a cubic perovskite with complex multiple-Q magnetic phases. Using field-orientation-dependent phase diagrams and an effective spin Hamiltonian (including single-ion anisotropy, bilinear/biquadratic interactions), the authors identify magnetoelastic signatures of a first-order valence transition at 40 T due to suppression of negative charge transfer, highlighting electronic itinerancy from ligand-hole band formation as key to stabilizing multiple-Q phases.
AI.motivation: To resolve the unresolved microscopic mechanism underlying the emergence of versatile multiple-Q magnetic phases in centrosymmetric itinerant magnet SrFeO₃.
AI.method: Field-orientation dependence of the magnetic phase diagram is elucidated; an effective spin Hamiltonian is established incorporating cubic single-ion anisotropy with bilinear and biquadratic interactions in momentum space; magnetoelastic signatures are observed.
AI.result: Magnetoelastic signatures of a first-order valence transition upon entering the forced FM phase at 40 T, attributed to suppression of negative charge transfer.
AI.conclusion: Electronic itinerancy arising from ligand-hole band formation is pivotally important for stabilizing multiple-Q phases.

title: High-field Magnetotransport Studies of Surface Conducting Diamonds
summary: The observation of strong and tunable spin-orbit interaction (SOI) in surface conducting diamond opens up a new avenue for building diamond-based spintronics. Herein we provide a comprehensive method to analyze the magnetotransport behavior of surface conducting hydrogen-terminated diamond (H-diamond) Hall bar devices and Al/Al2O3/V2O5/H-diamond MOSFETs, respectively. By adopting a significantly improved theoretical magneto transport model, the reduced magnetoconductance can be accurately explained both within and outside the quantum diffusive regime. The model is valid for all doping strategies of surface conducting diamond tested. From this analysis, we find that the orbital magnetoresistance, a classical effect distinct from the SOI, dominates the magnetotransport in surface conducting diamond at high magnetic fields. Furthermore, local hole mobilities as high as 1000 ~ 3000 cm2/Vs have been observed in this work, indicating the possibility of diamond-based electronics with ultra-high hole mobilities at cryogenic temperatures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical magnetotransport model for surface conducting hydrogen-terminated diamond, demonstrating that tunable spin-orbit interaction and orbital magnetoresistance dominate transport behavior, with local hole mobilities reaching 1000-3000 cm²/Vs at cryogenic temperatures.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive and accurate magnetotransport analysis framework for surface conducting H-diamond devices, enabling the understanding of spin-orbit interaction and electron transport mechanisms for building diamond-based spintronics and electronics.
AI.method: A significantly improved theoretical magnetotransport model was adopted to analyze reduced magnetoconductance in both Hall bar devices and Al/Al2O3/V2O5/H-diamond MOSFETs, valid across all doping strategies and both within and outside the quantum diffusive regime.
AI.result: Orbital magnetoresistance (a classical effect) dominates magnetotransport at high magnetic fields, distinct from spin-orbit interaction. Local hole mobilities as high as 1000-3000 cm²/Vs were observed at cryogenic temperatures.
AI.conclusion: The validated model and observed ultra-high hole mobilities indicate the strong potential for diamond-based spintronics and ultra-high hole mobility electronics at cryogenic temperatures.

title: Quantum Batteries in two-dimensional material-based Josephson Junctions
summary: We investigate the solid-state implementation of a Dicke-like quantum battery consisting of a two-dimensional material-based Josephson junction inductively coupled to a resonator, using graphene as a representative example. In this configuration, Andreev bound states naturally act as non-interacting, energetically non-degenerate two-level systems, and the setup allows for both single-photon and two-photon resonant processes. The coupling between the LC-circuit flux and the supercurrent through the junction gives rise to peculiar longitudinal interaction terms that have no counterpart in the conventional Dicke model. These additional couplings can enhance energy storage for a proper range of parameters. The proposed architecture also enables an alternative, but equivalent, charging protocol that relies on tuning the superconducting phase difference across the junction.

AI.tldr: A solid-state Dicke-like quantum battery is proposed using a graphene-based Josephson junction coupled to a resonator, where Andreev bound states act as two-level systems. The setup features longitudinal interactions absent in the conventional Dicke model, which can enhance energy storage, and enables charging via tuning the superconducting phase difference.
AI.motivation: To explore a solid-state realization of a Dicke-like quantum battery using two-dimensional materials (graphene) and investigate how unique longitudinal coupling terms can improve energy storage performance.
AI.method: A Josephson junction based on two-dimensional material (graphene) is inductively coupled to an LC resonator. Andreev bound states serve as two-level systems, enabling single-photon and two-photon resonant processes. The coupling between LC-circuit flux and supercurrent generates longitudinal interaction terms beyond the standard Dicke model.
AI.result: The longitudinal coupling terms, absent in the conventional Dicke model, can enhance energy storage for appropriate parameter ranges. An alternative charging protocol by tuning the superconducting phase difference is also presented.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture provides a viable solid-state platform for quantum battery implementation with enhanced energy storage capabilities and flexible charging mechanisms.

title: CNN-Based Classifier for Automated Identification of Magnetic States in Spin Dynamics Simulations
summary: The identification and classification of different magnetic states are essential for understanding the complex behavior of magnetic systems. Traditional approaches that rely on handcrafted features or manual inspection often fall short, particularly when dealing with subtle or topologically complex spin textures. In this study, we present an automated deep learning model that employs an EfficientNetV1B0 Convolutional Neural Network to classify nine distinct magnetic states, including both ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM) spin textures such as AFM skyrmions and AFM stripe domains. The spin configurations are generated through atomistic spin dynamics simulations using the Spirit code, then visualized with VFRendering to produce RGB images, which serve as inputs to the classification model.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an EfficientNetV1B0 CNN model to classify nine magnetic states (including FM and AFM spin textures like AFM skyrmions and stripe domains) from RGB images generated from atomistic spin dynamics simulations.
AI.motivation: Traditional handcrafted features and manual inspection are insufficient for identifying subtle or topologically complex spin textures, motivating the need for an automated deep learning approach.
AI.method: The authors use atomistic spin dynamics simulations (Spirit code) to generate spin configurations, which are visualized as RGB images via VFRendering. These images are classified using an EfficientNetV1B0 Convolutional Neural Network into nine distinct magnetic states.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract, but the approach successfully classifies nine magnetic states including both FM and AFM textures.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning (EfficientNetV1B0) provides an automated and effective solution for classifying complex magnetic spin textures beyond traditional manual or feature-based methods.

title: Transport Enhancement and In Situ Control of Electronic Correlation via Photoinduced Modulation Doping of van der Waals Heterostructures
summary: Modulation doping, a well-established technique for traditional semiconductor heterostructures, is a promising approach for tailoring carrier concentration in 2D materials devices. In this letter we report on photoinduced modulation doping in hBN-graphene-hBN-SiO2 heterostructures utilizing standard white light sources and no additional fabrication complexity. We establish the use of this technique to both dope the channel material and to photoanneal devices, providing control over electronic doping and disorder in the graphene channel. We analyze the transport properties by employing Drude and Landauer transport models, highlighting the ability to reversibly tune the mobility and mean scattering length of the graphene with a high degree of accuracy. This tunability allows us to switch our device between the diffusive and quasi-ballistic transport regimes in situ. We utilize the exceptional control our technique provides over local disorder to realize quantum Hall isospin ferromagnetic states in a device whose initial quality would otherwise leave such states unobservable. These results demonstrate precise manipulation of carrier density and charge disorder in van der Waals heterostructures, providing a highly accessible approach to creating high-quality devices capable of realizing correlated electronic states.

AI.tldr: Photoinduced modulation doping using white light enables reversible tuning of carrier density and disorder in hBN-graphene heterostructures, allowing switching between diffusive and quasi-ballistic transport and observation of quantum Hall isospin ferromagnetic states.
AI.motivation: To develop a simple, accessible technique for controlling carrier concentration and disorder in 2D materials without additional fabrication complexity, enabling high-quality devices for correlated electronic states.
AI.method: Photoinduced modulation doping in hBN-graphene-hBN-SiO2 heterostructures using standard white light sources; transport analysis via Drude and Landauer models.
AI.result: Reversible tuning of mobility and mean scattering length with high accuracy; in-situ switching between diffusive and quasi-ballistic transport; realization of quantum Hall isospin ferromagnetic states in initially low-quality devices.
AI.conclusion: Photoinduced modulation doping provides precise manipulation of carrier density and charge disorder in van der Waals heterostructures, offering a highly accessible route to creating high-quality devices for correlated electronic states.

title: Nonlinear Magnon Magnetic Moment Transport in Triangular-Lattice f-Wave Antialtermagnets
summary: We study the spin excitations in the frustrated coplanar 120-degree ground state of the triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet and demonstrate that they carry a magnetic moment perpendicular to the plane in which the spins order, despite the ground-state sublattice moments having no out-of-plane component. The symmetry of the momentum dependence of the magnetic moment and energy of the magnons renders the system an odd-parity f-wave magnet. Extending this model to a stack of antiferromagnetically coupled triangular layers provides a realization of magnons in a three-dimensional f-wave antialtermagnet. We show that nonlinear thermal transport effects of magnons, such as Edelstein and spin-splitter effects, provide clear experimental signatures of magnons in f-wave antialtermagnets.

AI.tldr: Spin excitations in the 120° ordered triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet carry an out-of-plane magnetic moment despite planar ground-state order, making it an odd-parity f-wave magnet; stacked layers form a 3D f-wave antialtermagnet, with nonlinear magnon thermal transport (Edelstein, spin-splitter effects) as experimental signatures.
AI.motivation: To characterize the magnetic moment of spin excitations in frustrated triangular-lattice antiferromagnets and to identify a new class of magnetic materials (f-wave antialtermagnets) with distinct experimental signatures via nonlinear thermal transport.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of spin excitations in the coplanar 120° ground state of the triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet; extension to stacked layers with antiferromagnetic interlayer coupling to form a 3D f-wave antialtermagnet; analysis of nonlinear thermal transport (Edelstein and spin-splitter effects).
AI.result: Magnons in the 120° ordered triangular-lattice antiferromagnet carry an out-of-plane magnetic moment with odd-parity f-wave symmetry; stacking yields a 3D f-wave antialtermagnet; nonlinear thermal transport effects provide clear experimental signals.
AI.conclusion: The triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet hosts f-wave magnons, and its stacked version realizes a 3D f-wave antialtermagnet with experimentally accessible nonlinear thermal transport signatures.

title: Theory-Guided, Machine-Learning-Accelerated Discovery of a 3D Carbon Nested Nodal-Surface Semimetal
summary: Extending the Dirac physics of two-dimensional (2D) graphene into three dimensions (3D) carbon allotropes with higher-dimensional band degeneracies remains a central challenge in topological materials science. Here, we propose a general symmetry-engineering principle that systematically transforms graphene's Dirac cone into a 3D nodal surface via controlled layering and registry shift, and employ this principle to guide a machine-learning-accelerated inverse design. By integrating a crystal diffusion variational autoencoder(CDVAE) with a Crystal Transformer, we discover a novel, dynamically and mechanically stable carbon allotrope named \textbf{Netsene} (bct-C$_{24}$), which crystallizes in the body-centered tetragonal \textit{I4/mcm} space group. First-principles calculations confirm that Netsene is a unique nested nodal-surface semimetal: it hosts a complex, double-bowl-shaped nodal-surface system around the Fermi level, protected by non-symmorphic symmetries, alongside Dirac-like linear crossings with Fermi velocities comparable to graphene ($\sim 9 \times 10^5$~m/s). Its non-trivial bulk topology manifests in drumhead surface states, including a nearly flat band. Netsene provides a structurally robust, bulk platform that unifies ultrahigh carrier mobility, topological nodal surfaces, and potential correlation physics, demonstrating the power of theory-guided, machine-learning-accelerated discovery for engineering topological quantum phases.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a symmetry-engineering principle to extend graphene's 2D Dirac cone to a 3D nodal surface and uses machine-learning-accelerated inverse design (CDVAE + Crystal Transformer) to discover Netsene (bct-C$_{24}$), a dynamically stable carbon allotrope with a nested nodal-surface semimetal phase, high Fermi velocity, drumhead surface states, and potential for topological and correlation physics.
AI.motivation: Extending the Dirac physics of 2D graphene into 3D carbon allotropes with higher-dimensional band degeneracies remains a central challenge in topological materials science.
AI.method: The authors propose a symmetry-engineering principle to transform graphene's 2D Dirac cone into a 3D nodal surface via controlled layering and registry shift, and integrate a crystal diffusion variational autoencoder (CDVAE) with a Crystal Transformer for machine-learning-accelerated inverse design.
AI.result: Discovery of Netsene (bct-C$_{24}$), a carbon allotrope in the body-centered tetragonal \textit{I4/mcm} space group. It is a nested nodal-surface semimetal with double-bowl-shaped nodal surfaces near the Fermi level protected by non-symmorphic symmetries, Dirac-like crossings with Fermi velocities $\sim 9 \times 10^5$ m/s, and drumhead surface states including a nearly flat band.
AI.conclusion: Netsene provides a structurally robust bulk platform unifying ultrahigh carrier mobility, topological nodal surfaces, and potential correlation physics, demonstrating the power of theory-guided, machine-learning-accelerated discovery for engineering topological quantum phases.

title: High-throughput study of electrical conductivity in ordered metals
summary: We present a computational framework that integrates machine learning with high-throughput \textit{ab initio} calculations to screen over 2.8 million compounds for metallic transport. We identify several intermetallic candidates with predicted high conductivities comparable to that of aluminum ($36.59 \times 10^6$~S/m). We perform full electron--phonon coupling calculations for the top-performing materials, yielding results in excellent agreement with available experimental data. Our analysis reveals that while the noble metals (Ag, Au, Cu) define the practical ceiling for conductivity due to their unique electronic structure and low scattering, compounds like $\text{LiBePt}_2$ can achieve comparable performance by utilizing valence electrons from light elements to shift high-scattering $d$-states beneath the Fermi level. This study not only identifies novel high-performance conductors but also demonstrates the predictive power of combining statistical learning with detailed ab initio calculations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a computational framework combining machine learning and ab initio calculations to screen over 2.8 million compounds for metallic conductivity, identifying intermetallic candidates with performance comparable to aluminum. Detailed electron-phonon coupling calculations confirm predictions, and reveal that compounds like LiBePt₂ can approach noble metal conductivity by using light-element valence electrons to shift high-scattering d-states below the Fermi level.
AI.motivation: To discover novel high-conductivity metallic materials beyond traditional noble metals by leveraging computational screening at scale, addressing the need for alternatives with comparable or superior electrical transport properties.
AI.method: Integrated machine learning with high-throughput ab initio calculations to screen over 2.8 million compounds; performed full electron-phonon coupling calculations for top-performing candidates; analyzed electronic structure to understand conductivity mechanisms.
AI.result: Identified several intermetallic candidates with predicted conductivities comparable to aluminum (36.59 × 10⁶ S/m); electron-phonon coupling calculations matched experimental data; discovered that LiBePt₂ achieves high conductivity by using light-element valence electrons to shift d-states below the Fermi level.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates the predictive power of combining statistical learning with detailed ab initio calculations for materials discovery, identifies novel high-performance conductors, and reveals that noble metals define the practical conductivity ceiling due to their unique electronic structure and low scattering.

title: Toward the Rational Design of Molecular Field-Coupled Nanocomputing Candidates
summary: Molecular Field-Coupled Nanocomputing (MolFCN) is a promising beyond-CMOS paradigm in which information is propagated electrostatically rather than through charge transport, enabling ultra-low-power logic. Identifying molecules with stable logic states, efficient clock-field switching, and reliable information propagation, however, remains an open challenge. In this Letter, we introduce LUFFY (Layered Unified Framework for MolFCN systematic analYsis), a framework for the rational design and validation of molecular candidates for MolFCN architectures. Starting from 27 synthetically accessible molecules, we combine conformational sampling and electrostatic analysis in neutral and oxidized states to derive robust descriptors of molecular response. In particular, we extract the V${in}$-to-Aggregated-Charge Transcharacteristics (VACTs), capturing the field-induced charge response, and introduce energy-averaged models validated via ab initio molecular dynamics to account for conformational diversity. Finally, we use the resulting molecular responses to evaluate device-level propagation and demonstrate stable information transfer. These results directly link molecular structure to functional information flow, identifying conformationally robust electrostatic response as a key requirement for MolFCN operation. Overall, this work establishes a unified and transferable framework for the identification and validation of MolFCN molecular candidates, bridging molecular design and circuit-level functionality. By unifying previously fragmented approaches into a sustainable methodology, LUFFY enables rational and scalable molecular discovery and establishes a foundation for data-driven design strategies that accelerate the development of ultra-low-power information processing technologies.

AI.tldr: LUFFY is a unified framework for systematically designing and validating molecular candidates for Molecular Field-Coupled Nanocomputing (MolFCN), linking molecular structure to stable information propagation via electrostatic response analysis.
AI.motivation: Identifying molecules with stable logic states, efficient clock-field switching, and reliable information propagation for ultra-low-power MolFCN remains an open challenge due to fragmented approaches.
AI.method: Starting from 27 synthetically accessible molecules, LUFFY combines conformational sampling and electrostatic analysis in neutral and oxidized states to derive robust molecular response descriptors, including VACTs (V_in-to-Aggregated-Charge Transcharacteristics) and energy-averaged models validated via ab initio molecular dynamics.
AI.result: The extracted molecular responses enable device-level propagation evaluation, demonstrating stable information transfer. Conformationally robust electrostatic response is identified as a key requirement for MolFCN operation.
AI.conclusion: LUFFY establishes a unified, transferable, and sustainable framework bridging molecular design and circuit-level functionality, enabling rational and scalable molecular discovery for ultra-low-power information processing technologies.

title: Spintronic Neuromorphic Hardware Using Domain Wall Based Neurons and Quantized Synapses
summary: In this work, we simulate the functionality of artificial neuron and synapse using spin-orbit torque-based spintronic devices and implemented a fully connected artificial neural netwrok (ANN). These neuro-synaptic devices are emulated using transverse domain wall dynamics in a rectangular magnetic nanotrack comprised of heavy metal/ferromagnet (HM/FM) heterostructures. The ReLU activation function of the neuron has been mimicked using the domain wall motion induced by a 3 ns current pulse. The synapse has been modelled using current-induced domain wall (DW) dynamics through a corrugated HM/FM nanotrack under the influence of a 10 ns current pulse with varying current density. The semicircular corrugations are in the form of notches, which are symmetrically located on both sides of the nanotrack. By applying 10 ns current pulses of varying densities, we achieve controlled DW pinning, revealing a step-like motion caused by temporary pauses at each pinning center. The electrical conductance of the pinned DW across various pinning points, act as stable synaptic weights for our ANN. Furthermore, we observe a threshold-dependent delay effect where each depinning event is influenced by previous ones, successfully mimicking synaptic memory and adaptability in neuromorphic systems. The fully connected ANN has been modeled using the conventional float32 synaptic weights for the MNIST and Fashion MNIST datasets with an accuracy of ~97 % and ~86 %, respectively, which serves as a test bed of our neuromorphic simulations. With the aim of implementing a sparse and low memory footprint ANN, we quantize the trained synaptic weights into discrete quantized level and tested the network, which demonstrate an accuracy of ~95% and ~62%, for the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST dataset, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a spintronic-based artificial neuron and synapse using spin-orbit torque-driven domain wall dynamics in HM/FM nanotracks, and implements a fully connected ANN for MNIST and Fashion MNIST classification, achieving ~97% and ~86% accuracy with float32 weights, and ~95% and ~62% accuracy with quantized weights.
AI.motivation: To simulate artificial neuron and synapse functionality using spin-orbit torque-based spintronic devices to implement energy-efficient neuromorphic computing with hardware-level neuro-synaptic emulation.
AI.method: Transverse domain wall dynamics in rectangular HM/FM magnetic nanotracks; ReLU neuron activation via 3 ns current pulse-induced DW motion; synapse modeled via current-induced DW dynamics in corrugated nanotracks with semicircular notches using 10 ns current pulses; quantized weight pruning for low memory footprint.
AI.result: ANN achieves ~97% (MNIST) and ~86% (Fashion MNIST) accuracy with float32 weights; quantized weights yield ~95% (MNIST) and ~62% (Fashion MNIST) accuracy. Threshold-dependent depinning delay mimics synaptic memory and adaptability.
AI.conclusion: The spintronic neuro-synaptic devices can effectively emulate biological neural functions, and the quantized weight scheme enables sparse, low-memory neuromorphic systems with competitive accuracy on standard benchmarks.

title: Delineating the interplay effects of microstructure topology and residual stresses in ultrafast laser irradiated thin films
summary: Advanced nanodevices require high-precision machining of thin films using ultrafast lasers. However, thin-film fabrications cause variations in microstructure, crystallographic orientation, and residual stresses owing to coating conditions and substrate choice. This work investigates the complex interplay between these factors in ultrafast laser-irradiated gold (Au) thin films using a hybrid Two Temperature Model-Molecular Dynamics simulations. We realized microstructure-informed atomistic models with varying grain topologies (randomized vs. equiaxed), grain sizes, and residual tensile/compressive stress configurations. Our results reveal a clear hierarchy of influence on laser-metal interaction: 1.) Microstructure configuration 2.) Topology 3.) Grain Size 4.) Crystallographic orientations. In fine-grained thin films, grain boundaries act as primary melting precursors, while local crystallographic orientation determines the melting extent in coarser grains. Residual tensile stresses contribute to higher melting and greater laser-induced expansion than unstrained films. Conversely, residual compressive stresses resist deformation, as deposited thermal energy is utilized to overcome lattice compression, leading to reduced expansion. We found that microstructure grain topology and size exert a stronger fingerprint on film expansion than the initial defect density.

AI.tldr: This study uses hybrid Two Temperature Model-Molecular Dynamics simulations to investigate how microstructure variations (grain topology, size, residual stresses, crystallographic orientation) affect ultrafast laser interactions with gold thin films, revealing a hierarchy of influence where microstructure configuration > topology > grain size > crystallographic orientation.
AI.motivation: Advanced nanodevices require high-precision thin film machining using ultrafast lasers, but thin-film fabrications cause uncontrolled variations in microstructure, crystallographic orientation, and residual stresses that affect laser processing outcomes.
AI.method: Hybrid Two Temperature Model-Molecular Dynamics (TTM-MD) simulations with microstructure-informed atomistic models incorporating varying grain topologies (randomized vs. equiaxed), grain sizes, and residual tensile/compressive stress configurations.
AI.result: Microstructure configuration is the dominant factor, followed by topology, grain size, and crystallographic orientations. Grain boundaries act as primary melting precursors in fine-grained films; crystallographic orientation determines melting extent in coarser grains. Tensile stresses increase melting/expansion; compressive stresses resist deformation.
AI.conclusion: Microstructure grain topology and size have a stronger influence on film expansion than initial defect density, providing a clear hierarchy for optimizing ultrafast laser processing of thin films.

title: Monitored quantum transport through a disordered one-dimensional conductor
summary: We formulate a quantum master equation for the many-particle density matrix of electrons propagating through a single-mode conductor, combining elastic scattering by disorder with time-resolved projective measurements that monitor the outcome of scattering events. The full counting statistics of transmitted electrons has a binomial distribution function, whose mean ${\cal T}$ and variance ${\cal T}(1-{\cal T})$ determine the conductance and shot noise power, respectively. Monitoring suppresses the phase coherence responsible for one-dimensional localization: The decay with conductor length $L$ of the typical transmission probability crosses over at $L\simeq \ell_φ$ from the exponential $e^{-L/ξ}$ (with localization length $ξ$) to the Ohmic $1/L$ decay. Numerical solution of the master equation gives, for weak monitoring, a logarithmic dependence $\ell_φ\simeq ξ\ln(v_{\rm F}τ_φ/ξ)$ of the coherence length $\ell_φ$ on the mean time $τ_φ$ between measurements.

AI.tldr: A quantum master equation is formulated for electrons in a single-mode conductor, combining elastic scattering with time-resolved projective measurements. Monitoring suppresses phase coherence and causes a crossover from exponential (localized) to Ohmic (1/L) transmission decay, with the coherence length scaling logarithmically with measurement interval.
AI.motivation: To understand how continuous monitoring (projective measurements) affects the transmission statistics and localization behavior of electrons in a disordered conductor, particularly the crossover from Anderson localization to Ohmic transport.
AI.method: A quantum master equation for the many-particle density matrix is formulated, combining elastic scattering by disorder with time-resolved projective measurements. The full counting statistics is analyzed, and numerical solutions are obtained to study the crossover behavior.
AI.result: The full counting statistics is binomial with mean T and variance T(1-T). Monitoring suppresses phase coherence, causing a crossover from exponential decay e^{-L/ξ} to Ohmic 1/L decay at L≈ℓ_φ. The coherence length ℓ_φ ≈ ξ ln(v_F τ_φ/ξ) depends logarithmically on the measurement interval τ_φ.
AI.conclusion: Monitoring destroys one-dimensional localization by suppressing phase coherence, leading to Ohmic transport beyond a coherence length that scales logarithmically with measurement frequency.

title: Virp: neural network-accelerated prediction of physical properties in site-disordered materials
summary: Among metallic alloys, ceramics, and even common compounds such as water ice, it is usual to find materials in which crystalline order is expressed as a probability. In such cases, one or more sites within a crystal can be occupied by multiple elements or vacancies, according to a set of probabilities. These crystal structures remain inaccessible to common first-principles materials simulation methodologies, which assumes perfect crystal order. Workaround strategies to this limitation include quasirandom structures and cluster expansion. These methods are system-specific and computationally expensive as they rely on large scale Monte Carlo simulations of enlarged unit cells. To address these limitations, we propose a pipeline combining a permutation-based virtual cell generation algorithm, sampling regime, and thermodynamic post-processing which greatly improves the feasibility of computation analyses for site-disordered materials. We demonstrate that the massive configurational space can be adequately sampled with 400 virtual cells, as long as the supercell definition is sufficiently large.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a pipeline using permutation-based virtual cell generation, sampling, and thermodynamic post-processing to efficiently simulate site-disordered materials, demonstrating adequate sampling with 400 virtual cells given sufficiently large supercell definitions.
AI.motivation: Common first-principles methods assume perfect crystal order and cannot handle site-disordered materials where sites are occupied by multiple elements or vacancies probabilistically. Existing workarounds (quasirandom structures, cluster expansion) are system-specific and computationally expensive due to reliance on large-scale Monte Carlo simulations of enlarged unit cells.
AI.method: A pipeline combining (1) a permutation-based virtual cell generation algorithm, (2) a sampling regime, and (3) thermodynamic post-processing to improve computational feasibility for site-disordered materials.
AI.result: The massive configurational space of site-disordered materials can be adequately sampled with only 400 virtual cells, provided the supercell definition is sufficiently large.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline greatly improves the feasibility of computational analyses for site-disordered materials, overcoming the limitations of existing first-principles methodologies and workaround strategies.

title: Signatures of quantum chaos in phonon-polariton billiards
summary: We use scanning near-field optical microscopy to image hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) billiards with integrable and chaotic geometries. In Sinai billiards, we observe irregular mode patterns consistent with quantum scarring, together with an unexpected sensitivity to weak probe perturbations. These random-wave features coexist with non-chaotic one-dimensional boundary modes arising from nontrivial polariton reflection at the billiard edge. As the billiard boundary becomes increasingly complex, the Fourier transforms of the measured signals evolve toward ring-like structures consistent with Berry's random-wave conjecture. We develop a numerical framework based on the Helmholtz equation with generalized boundary conditions that encode angle-dependent reflection phase shifts. The calculated level statistics exhibit a crossover from Poisson-like behavior in integrable billiards to Wigner-Dyson-like behavior in chaotic geometries, with small deviations from the canonical form arising from nonlinear boundary conditions that require self-consistent bulk-boundary analysis. Theoretical analysis based on dissipative Green's functions qualitatively reproduces the near-field data. These results establish mesoscopic van der Waals billiards as a rich platform for studying generalized chaotic dynamics of hybrid light-matter polaritons.

AI.tldr: This paper uses scanning near-field optical microscopy to image hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hBN billiards with integrable and chaotic geometries, observing quantum scarring, random-wave features, and boundary modes. A numerical Helmholtz framework with generalized boundary conditions reproduces the crossover from Poisson to Wigner-Dyson level statistics, and dissipative Green's function theory matches experimental data, establishing van der Waals billiards as a platform for studying chaotic polariton dynamics.
AI.motivation: To explore chaotic dynamics of hybrid light-matter polaritons in mesoscopic van der Waals billiards by combining experimental near-field imaging with theoretical modeling.
AI.method: Scanning near-field optical microscopy (SNOM) imaging of hBN billiards; numerical Helmholtz equation with generalized angle-dependent boundary conditions; level statistics analysis; dissipative Green's function theoretical framework.
AI.result: Observed irregular mode patterns consistent with quantum scarring and weak probe sensitivity in Sinai billiards; coexistence of random-wave features with 1D boundary modes; Fourier transforms evolving toward ring-like structures matching Berry's random-wave conjecture; level statistics showing Poisson to Wigner-Dyson crossover with deviations from canonical forms due to nonlinear boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: Mesoscopic van der Waals billiards provide a rich platform for studying generalized chaotic dynamics of hybrid light-matter polaritons, with experimental and theoretical evidence of quantum chaos signatures in polariton systems.

title: Enrichment of rhombohedral stacking by mechanical exfoliation of graphite
summary: Rhombohedral (ABC) graphite hosts a surface-localized flat band that supports correlated and topological electronic phases, but its experimental study is limited by the scarcity of ABC stacking in natural graphite, which is dominated by Bernal (AB) stacking. Here we show that the routine mechanical exfoliation step itself enriches the rhombohedral content of graphite flakes, and that a simple blade-assisted exfoliation step, which introduces additional shear, amplifies the effect further. Using large-area Raman 2D-band skewness mapping we measure ABC content at area fractions of 3\% in the pristine source crystal, 16\% after conventional exfoliation, and 26\% after blade-assisted exfoliation for thick flakes. In thin flakes ($<20$ layers) the per-flake area fraction reaches 75\% in the upper tail of the distribution. Tracking individual flakes before and after blade-assisted exfoliation shows that wrinkles seed AB-ABC domain walls, and uniaxial strain can move these walls. Blade-assisted mechanical exfoliation therefore removes one of the bottlenecks to the preparation of ABC-rich graphite samples for studies of correlated and topological phases in rhombohedral graphite.

AI.tldr: Mechanical exfoliation enriches rhombohedral (ABC) stacking content in graphite flakes, especially when shear is applied via blade-assisted exfoliation, increasing ABC fraction from 3% (pristine) to 26% (thick flakes) and up to 75% in thin flakes.
AI.motivation: Rhombohedral (ABC) graphite hosts a surface-localized flat band supporting correlated and topological phases, but its study is hindered by the scarcity of ABC stacking in natural graphite, which is dominated by Bernal (AB) stacking.
AI.method: Large-area Raman 2D-band skewness mapping to measure ABC content; comparison of pristine source crystal, conventional exfoliation, and blade-assisted exfoliation; tracking individual flakes before and after blade-assisted exfoliation.
AI.result: ABC content: 3% in pristine source, 16% after conventional exfoliation, 26% after blade-assisted exfoliation for thick flakes; up to 75% per-flake area fraction in thin flakes (<20 layers). Wrinkles seed AB-ABC domain walls; uniaxial strain moves these walls.
AI.conclusion: Blade-assisted mechanical exfoliation removes a key bottleneck in preparing ABC-rich graphite samples for studying correlated and topological phases in rhombohedral graphite.

title: Signatures of the Quantum Geometric Dipole of Interlayer Excitons in Counterflow Conductivity
summary: Collective excitations of many-body electron systems can carry internal structure, supporting novel quantum geometric and topological properties. Among these are a quantum geometric dipole (QGD), which for excitons have direct significance as an internal polarization. For interlayer excitons of a bilayer system, this represents an in-plane dipole moment, which can be used to drive them with in-plane electric fields. In this work, we consider counterflow electric currents associated with driven excitons in such a bilayer system as a probe of their QGD structure. As a simple but non-trivial example, we analyze a structure with a one-dimensional periodic potential in a strong perpendicular magnetic field. The resulting magnetoexciton bands host QGD structure that distinguishes it from the exciton QGD of a uniform system. To model exciton transport we adopt a Boltzmann approach that includes inter-band tunneling, allowing us to consider non-equilibrium momentum distributions that result from strong layer-antisymmetric driving fields. We show how linear response to a layer-symmetric component of the driving fields provide information about the QGD, and that the broad QGD structure of the exciton bands can be probed by the varying the layer-antisymmetric field. Our results demonstrate that counterflow conductivity serves as a tunable probe of the internal quantum geometric structure carried by the interlayer excitons, connecting transport to the quantum geometry of many-body excitations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using counterflow electric currents as a probe of the quantum geometric dipole (QGD) structure of interlayer excitons in bilayer systems, demonstrating through a model with 1D periodic potential and strong magnetic field that counterflow conductivity can reveal the QGD by varying layer-antisymmetric driving fields.
AI.motivation: Collective excitations (excitons) can carry quantum geometric and topological properties, specifically a quantum geometric dipole (QGD) representing internal polarization. For interlayer excitons, this QGD manifests as an in-plane dipole moment, but methods to probe this internal structure are needed.
AI.method: A bilayer system with a one-dimensional periodic potential in a strong perpendicular magnetic field is analyzed. The resulting magnetoexciton bands host QGD structure. A Boltzmann transport approach including inter-band tunneling is adopted to model exciton transport under strong layer-antisymmetric driving fields.
AI.result: Linear response to layer-symmetric driving fields provides information about the QGD. The broad QGD structure of exciton bands can be probed by varying the layer-antisymmetric field. Counterflow conductivity serves as a tunable probe of the internal quantum geometric structure.
AI.conclusion: Counterflow conductivity is demonstrated to be a tunable probe of the internal quantum geometric dipole carried by interlayer excitons, connecting transport measurements to the quantum geometry of many-body excitations.

title: Odd-Parity Chiral Magnons in Collinear Antiferromagnetic Multiferroics: Symmetry Classification and Ferroelectric Switching
summary: The coupling between ferroelectrics and magnetism presents a promising avenue for low-dissipation spintronic devices. However, such couplings remain rare, and the direct realization of magnetic order driven by ferroelectric switching in insulators continues to pose a significant challenge. Here, we identify a class of collinear antiferromagnetic multiferroics in which intra-sublattice Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) induces odd-parity chiral magnons that are reversible via ferroelectric switching. Leveraging the charge-neutral nature of magnons, such multiferroics enable non-volatile ferroelectric control over magnon spin splitting, Hall transport, and spin polarization in antiferromagnetic insulators. Remarkably, magnetic group analysis and spin wave calculations reveal that the chiral splitting adopts three planar odd-parity forms, f-wave, p-wave, and fully-gapped types, with an intriguing Néel vector dependence. Furthermore, density functional theory calculations validate various material candidates, ranging from two-dimensional to bulk systems. Our work provides new insights into the realization of odd-parity chiral magnons in collinear antiferromagnets and opens new avenues for magnetoelectric coupling mechanisms in multiferroics

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a class of collinear antiferromagnetic multiferroics where intra-sublattice Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) generates odd-parity chiral magnons that can be switched via ferroelectric polarization. This enables non-volatile ferroelectric control over magnon spin splitting, Hall transport, and spin polarization in antiferromagnetic insulators, with three planar odd-parity forms (f-wave, p-wave, fully-gapped) exhibiting Néel vector dependence, validated by DFT for 2D to bulk candidates.
AI.motivation: The coupling between ferroelectrics and magnetism is promising for low-dissipation spintronic devices, but such couplings are rare and direct realization of magnetic order driven by ferroelectric switching in insulators remains a significant challenge.
AI.method: Magnetic group analysis, spin wave calculations, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to identify and characterize the class of collinear antiferromagnetic multiferroics with intra-sublattice DMI-induced odd-parity chiral magnons.
AI.result: Chiral splitting exhibits three planar odd-parity forms: f-wave, p-wave, and fully-gapped types, with a Néel vector dependence. Material candidates are validated from 2D to bulk systems.
AI.conclusion: The work provides new insights into realizing odd-parity chiral magnons in collinear antiferromagnets and opens new avenues for magnetoelectric coupling mechanisms in multiferroics.

title: Photoemission intermittency via stochastic gating in rubrene nanowires coupled to plasmonic silver nanoparticles
summary:
In this work, we report a new nanoscale phenomenon observed as photoemission intermittency (On-Off electron emission), manifested as stochastic bursts in electron yield at quasi-one-dimensional organic wires and silver nanoparticles interface. Energy-resolved measurements reveal that the emitted electrons carry out hybrid information, containing photoelectron yield enhancement associated with the nanoparticles and kinetic energies determined by the organic semiconductor. The intermittency results in a dynamic shift of the electron spectra correlating with the photoelectron yield. We attribute the observed behaviour to the photo-hole accumulation and stochastic gating of charge due to electron-hole separation at the nano interface. These findings introduces the photoemission intermittency as a nanoscale phenomenon indicating a new dynamic regime of charge assisted emission at organic-plasmonic interfaces.
  Keywords: rubrene, nanoparticle, PEEM, exciton, charge

AI.tldr: The paper reports a newly observed nanoscale phenomenon called photoemission intermittency (On-Off electron emission) at organic wire-silver nanoparticle interfaces, characterized by stochastic bursts in electron yield. The emitted electrons carry hybrid information combining photoelectron yield enhancement from nanoparticles and kinetic energies from the organic semiconductor. The effect is attributed to photo-hole accumulation and stochastic charge gating from electron-hole separation, revealing a dynamic regime of charge-assisted emission at organic-plasmonic interfaces.
AI.motivation: To discover and characterize a previously unreported nanoscale phenomenon of photoemission intermittency at organic-plasmonic nano-interfaces, and to understand its underlying physical mechanism involving charge dynamics.
AI.method: Energy-resolved photoemission measurements of quasi-one-dimensional organic wires (rubrene) at silver nanoparticle interfaces, analyzing stochastic bursts in electron yield and spectral shifts correlating with photoelectron yield.
AI.result: Observation of stochastic On-Off electron emission bursts; hybrid information carried by emitted electrons (yield enhancement from nanoparticles, kinetic energies from organic semiconductor); dynamic spectral shifts correlated with photoelectron yield.
AI.conclusion: Photoemission intermittency is a nanoscale phenomenon revealing a new dynamic regime of charge-assisted emission at organic-plasmonic interfaces, driven by photo-hole accumulation and stochastic gating of charge due to electron-hole separation.

title: Generation of an anomalous linearly dispersing spin-polarized band in Bi-based topological insulators
summary: We report the generation of an anomalous linearly dispersing, spin-polarized band in Bi-based topological insulator (TI) thin films, induced by soft Ar-ion bombardment followed by annealing. This extra band -- which we call the anomalous linearly dispersing state (ALS) -- is superimposed on the regular band structure including the topological surface state (TSS), spans an unusually large energetic range of up to ${\sim}\,\SI{650}{\milli\electronvolt}$ at the $Γ$-point, and appears near the Fermi energy. Spin-resolved measurements indicate spin-momentum locking with a helicity \emph{opposite} to that of the regular TSS. The Fermi velocity of the ALS, $v_\mathrm{F} = (5.1\pm 0.4)\times 10^{5}\,\frac m s$, is indistinguishable from that of the regular TSS, $(5.3\pm 0.5)\times 10^{5}\,\frac m s$. The observation is reproducible across samples of varying thickness and was confirmed at two independent synchrotron radiation facilities. We discuss different mechanisms for the physical origin of the observed ALS including sputtering-induced TSS relocation, bi-layer formation by,e.g., chalcogen removal, and high-index surface relocation.

AI.tldr: Ar-ion bombardment of Bi-based topological insulator thin films creates an anomalous linearly dispersing state (ALS) — a spin-polarized band with opposite helicity to the topological surface state, spanning ~650 meV at the Γ-point with comparable Fermi velocity (~5×10⁵ m/s), reproducible across samples and facilities.
AI.motivation: To investigate how controlled surface modification (Ar-ion bombardment + annealing) alters the electronic structure of Bi-based topological insulator thin films, particularly to discover and characterize an unexpected linearly dispersing spin-polarized band.
AI.method: Soft Ar-ion bombardment followed by annealing on Bi-based TI thin films; spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to probe electronic structure and spin texture; measurements at two independent synchrotron facilities across samples of varying thickness.
AI.result: An anomalous linearly dispersing state (ALS) emerges superimposed on the regular band structure, spanning ~650 meV at Γ-point near the Fermi energy. The ALS exhibits spin-momentum locking with helicity opposite to the regular topological surface state. Its Fermi velocity v_F = (5.1±0.4)×10⁵ m/s is statistically indistinguishable from the TSS's v_F = (5.3±0.5)×10⁵ m/s.
AI.conclusion: The ALS is a reproducible phenomenon induced by Ar-ion bombardment. Possible origins include sputtering-induced TSS relocation, bi-layer formation via chalcogen removal, or high-index surface relocation, but the exact mechanism remains to be determined.

title: Antiferromagnetic Ordering Enhanced Magnetic Damping in Mn2Au/CoFeB Bilayers
summary: Antiferromagnets (AFMs) hold significant potential for spintronic devices owing to their insensitivity to external magnetic fields and the absence of stray fields. Beyond these inherent advantages, an AFM can manipulate the magnetic dynamics of a ferromagnet (FM) layer in AFM/FM bilayers, whereas the mechanism of such manipulation remains controversial. Here, we investigate the magnetic dynamics of AFM/FM Mn2Au/CoFeB bilayers via Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR). It is found that the Néel temperature of 2-nm-thick Mn2Au is as low as ~40 K, in sharp contrast to that of bulk Mn2Au, which exceeds 1000 K. In the Mn2Au(2 nm)/CoFeB(4 nm) bilayer, the magnetic damping $α$ of the CoFeB layer increases from 0.013 to 0.047 as temperature decreases from 160 K to 10 K, accompanied by a synchronous increase in the exchange coupling field H_rot. Such an increase in $α$ is attributed to the enhanced spin angular momentum transfer from CoFeB to Mn2Au, mediated through AFM-FM exchange coupling between Mn2Au and CoFeB, which is enhanced by the Mn2Au antiferromagnetic ordering as the temperature decreases. Our study provides deeper insights into AFM/FM dynamics and spintronic storage technology.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates AFM/FM bilayers (Mn2Au/CoFeB) via FMR, finding that the Néel temperature of ultrathin Mn2Au drops dramatically (~40 K vs >1000 K bulk), and magnetic damping increases with decreasing temperature due to enhanced exchange coupling and spin angular momentum transfer from FM to AFM.
AI.motivation: To resolve the controversy surrounding the mechanism by which antiferromagnets manipulate the magnetic dynamics of ferromagnet layers in AFM/FM bilayers.
AI.method: Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) measurements on Mn2Au/CoFeB bilayers with varying temperature, analyzing magnetic damping and exchange coupling fields.
AI.result: The Néel temperature of 2-nm-thick Mn2Au is ~40 K (vs >1000 K bulk); magnetic damping α of CoFeB increases from 0.013 to 0.047 as temperature drops from 160 K to 10 K, alongside a synchronous increase in exchange coupling field H_rot.
AI.conclusion: The increased magnetic damping is attributed to enhanced spin angular momentum transfer from CoFeB to Mn2Au, mediated by AFM-FM exchange coupling that strengthens with Mn2Au antiferromagnetic ordering at lower temperatures, providing deeper insights for AFM/FM dynamics and spintronic storage technology.

title: Harnessing Linear and Nonlinear Optical Responses in Ferroelectric LaMoN$_3$ for Enhanced Photovoltaic Efficiency
summary: Nitride perovskites are an emerging class of materials predicted to exhibit diverse functional properties, yet remain underexplored due to synthesis challenges of oxygen-free nitrides. Recently, LaMoN$_3$ has been reported as an oxygen-free nitride perovskite with polar symmetry, exhibiting excellent dynamic stability and ferroelectric properties under moderate pressure. However, its phase stability, linear and non-linear optical response, excitonic and polaronic behavior, and efficiency under high pressure remain unexplored. Applying pressure enables systematic tuning of the electronic structure properties, thereby facilitating the identification of phases optimized for either linear or nonlinear optical responses. Therefore, in this work, we systematically investigate these properties of LaMoN$_3$ up to 40 GPa using first-principles methods, including density functional theory, density functional perturbation theory, many-body perturbation theory (namely G$_0$W$_0$ and BSE), and tight binding approximation model. Our study shows that LaMoN$_3$ remains dynamically stable and retains its single-phase structure up to 40 GPa. The compound exhibits an indirect bandgap that decreases from 2.17 eV (0 GPa) to 1.45 eV (40 GPa) at the G$_0$W$_0$@PBE level. Using the BSE, we find that pressure enhances the SLME while lowering the exciton binding energy, both favorable for photovoltaic applications. The bulk photovoltaic efficiency trend with pressure mimics the behavior of the shift current density J$_SC$ , peaking near 15 GPa before declining at higher pressures due to a diminished nonlinear shift current response. These results highlight pressure-tuned regimes to enhance photovoltaic performance. We thereby propose multi-junction device, combining absorber layers optimized for linear and nonlinear optical currents, together boosting solar energy conversion through complementary mechanisms.

AI.tldr: This first-principles study of LaMoN₃ under high pressure (up to 40 GPa) reveals it remains dynamically stable, with a tunable indirect bandgap (2.17→1.45 eV), pressure-enhanced SLME, reduced exciton binding energy, and peak shift current density near 15 GPa, leading to a proposed multi-junction device for improved photovoltaic efficiency.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate the unexplored phase stability, linear/nonlinear optical response, excitonic/polaronic behavior, and efficiency under high pressure of LaMoN₃, an oxygen-free nitride perovskite with promising ferroelectric properties, aiming to identify pressure-optimized phases for optical applications.
AI.method: First-principles methods: density functional theory (DFT), density functional perturbation theory (DFPT), many-body perturbation theory (G₀W₀ and BSE), and tight-binding approximation model, applied up to 40 GPa.
AI.result: LaMoN₃ remains dynamically stable and single-phase up to 40 GPa. Indirect bandgap decreases from 2.17 eV (0 GPa) to 1.45 eV (40 GPa) at G₀W₀@PBE level. Pressure enhances SLME and lowers exciton binding energy. Shift current density J_SC peaks near 15 GPa, then declines at higher pressures.
AI.conclusion: Pressure-tuned regimes can enhance photovoltaic performance. A multi-junction device combining absorber layers optimized for linear and nonlinear optical currents is proposed to boost solar energy conversion via complementary mechanisms.

title: A sulfonitride transparent conductive thin film with ultra-high refractive index
summary: With the rise of AI-assisted materials screening, extraordinary properties are now frequently predicted in experimentally uncharted material systems, highlighting the need to develop new synthesis methods for unconventional materials beyond the classic bulk powder form. Here, we establish the first thin-film growth route for any metal sulfonitride compound by realizing Zr2SN2 films with a rare and compelling combination of optical and electrical properties. Zr2SN2 is transparent across most of the visible range while exhibiting a very high average refractive index of 2.95 in the visible, exceeding expectations based on conventional refractive index-bandgap scaling. Importantly, the same Zr2SN2 film shows degenerate n-type conductivity with carrier density above 10^20 cm-3 and intragrain mobility above 8 cm2V-1s-1, approaching those of established transparent conductive oxides. Zr2SN2 thus demonstrates that strong light-matter interaction, optical transparency and electrical conductivity can be reconciled within a single material platform, revealing a new class of high-refractive-index transparent conductors.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the first thin-film growth route for metal sulfonitride (Zr2SN2) films, achieving a rare combination of high transparency across most of the visible range, a very high average refractive index of 2.95, and degenerate n-type conductivity with carrier density >10^20 cm-3 and intragrain mobility >8 cm2V-1s-1, demonstrating a new class of high-refractive-index transparent conductors.
AI.motivation: With AI-assisted materials screening predicting extraordinary properties in experimentally uncharted systems, there is a pressing need to develop new synthesis methods for unconventional materials beyond classic bulk powder forms, particularly for metal sulfonitride compounds.
AI.method: The authors established a thin-film growth route for Zr2SN2, a metal sulfonitride compound, enabling experimental realization of its optical and electrical properties.
AI.result: Zr2SN2 films exhibit: (1) transparency across most of the visible range, (2) a very high average refractive index of 2.95 in the visible (exceeding conventional refractive index-bandgap scaling), and (3) degenerate n-type conductivity with carrier density >10^20 cm-3 and intragrain mobility >8 cm2V-1s-1, approaching those of established transparent conductive oxides.
AI.conclusion: Zr2SN2 demonstrates that strong light-matter interaction, optical transparency, and electrical conductivity can be reconciled within a single material platform, revealing a new class of high-refractive-index transparent conductors.

title: Observation of magnetically switchable quantum geometric photocurrents
comment: The manuscript is a submitted version
summary: In non-centrosymmetric materials, light can be rectified into two types of DC photocurrents, known as injection and shift currents, through the bulk photovoltaic effect. Recent theory has uncovered their deep relation with the two-state quantum geometry of resonant transitions: In non-magnetic crystals, where these currents have been routinely observed, the injection current responds to circular light and probes the Berry curvature, while the shift current responds to linear light and probes the geometric connection. Magnetic crystals have been predicted to show a new set of hitherto unobserved magnetically switchable photocurrents, with the roles of linear and circular light interchanged: A linear injection current, which probes the quantum metric, and a circular shift current, which probes the geometric torsion. In this work, we demonstrate the existence of such currents for the first time, demonstrating the switching of the current by flipping the Néel vector in a van der Waals antiferromagnet. Furthermore, their specific frequency and temperature dependence confirm the assignment of circular shift and linear injection currents. Our work demonstrates a new way to control photocurrents in magnets that are directly tied to geometry and have promising applications in antiferromagnetic spintronics and light harvesting.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the first experimental observation of magnetically switchable photocurrents (linear injection and circular shift currents) in a van der Waals antiferromagnet, which are linked to quantum geometry and can be switched by flipping the Néel vector.
AI.motivation: While non-magnetic crystals exhibit injection (circular light, Berry curvature) and shift (linear light, geometric connection) currents, magnetic crystals were predicted to show new photocurrents with reversed light-current roles (linear injection, circular shift) tied to quantum metric and geometric torsion, but these had not been observed experimentally.
AI.method: Optical excitation experiments on a van der Waals antiferromagnet, measuring photocurrents while controlling the Néel vector orientation, and analyzing frequency and temperature dependence to distinguish circular shift and linear injection currents.
AI.result: Demonstrated the existence of linear injection current (probing quantum metric) and circular shift current (probing geometric torsion) for the first time, with switching behavior upon Néel vector reversal and characteristic frequency/temperature dependence.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a new mechanism for controlling photocurrents in magnets via quantum geometry, with potential applications in antiferromagnetic spintronics and light harvesting.

title: Upscaling DFT-trained machine-learning interatomic potential toward Quantum Monte Carlo accuracy: Sulfur-vacancy migration in monolayer MoS$_2$ as a testbed
comment: 11 pages, 8 pages main text, 3 pages supplementary, 10 figures in total, 6 figures in the main text, 4 figures in the supplementary
summary: We designed a procedure to train a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) at benchmark-quality quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) accuracy. To avoid the complexities of high-quality atomic force determination with the stochastic QMC methods, we use a multi-fidelity approach wherein high-level QMC energies are used alongside suitably processed low-level DFT atomic forces to train a QMC fine-tuned MLIP which significantly improves both the energetics and atomic forces over the baseline DFT-based MLIP. Fine-tuning is only applied to the readout layers of an equivariant message-passing MACE MLIP. We used sulfur mono- and multiple vacancies in monolayer MoS$_2$ as a testbed and demonstrate a near QMC accuracy of the model in a number of in- and out-of-domain tests. We show that a fairly limited dataset of QMC energies suffice to significantly improve the baseline DFT MLIP. The accuracy of our approach is demonstrated on energy and free energy migration barriers of mono- and multiple S-vacancy defects. The results open the window to large-scale near QMC quality simulations with large numbers of atoms and/or molecular dynamics configurations which would not be possible by a direct brute-force application of QMC methods.

AI.tldr: A multi-fidelity approach using QMC energies and DFT forces to fine-tune a MACE MLIP achieves near-QMC accuracy for monolayer MoS₂ vacancy simulations, enabling large-scale simulations previously infeasible with direct QMC methods.
AI.motivation: To achieve benchmark-quality QMC accuracy in MLIPs while avoiding the computational complexity and expense of stochastic QMC force calculations, enabling large-scale atomistic simulations with near-QMC fidelity.
AI.method: A multi-fidelity training procedure: high-level QMC energies are combined with low-level DFT atomic forces to fine-tune only the readout layers of an equivariant message-passing MACE MLIP, using sulfur mono- and multiple vacancies in monolayer MoS₂ as a test system.
AI.result: Near-QMC accuracy is achieved for both in-domain and out-of-domain tests, including energy and free energy migration barriers of mono- and multiple S-vacancy defects, with only a limited QMC energy dataset needed to significantly improve the baseline DFT MLIP.
AI.conclusion: This approach opens the door to large-scale near-QMC quality simulations (large atom counts and/or molecular dynamics) that are impossible with brute-force QMC methods directly.

title: A Local Probe Mass Spectrometer for Localized and Sensitive Product Detection in Environmental Electron Microscopy
summary: Aberration-corrected environmental transmission electron microscopy (ETEM) enables atomic-resolution imaging of dynamic catalytic processes. Correlating atomic-scale structural changes with reaction products detected by mass spectrometry offers a powerful route to uncover catalytic mechanisms. However, current approaches face fundamental limitations: closed-cell ETEM setups suffer from diffuse scattering by SiN windows, degrading spatial resolution and sensitivity, while open-cell configurations enable high-resolution imaging and maintain high sensitivity but suffer from significant dilution of reaction products during transport to the mass spectrometer (MS). To overcome these challenges, we develop a Local Probe Mass Spectrometer (LPMS) integrated with aberration-corrected ETEM. The setup combines a DENSsolution Stream holder with a MS. To preserve spatial resolution, both top and bottom SiN membranes of the MEMS chip are removed, while the gas environment is maintained via the ETEM chamber. Reaction products are sampled locally via a micro-capillary positioned near the catalyst and connected to a holder gas line that delivers the gas to the MS. Initial validation in environmental SEM confirmed controlled gas delivery to the MS. Co3O4 nanoplates serve as a model catalyst due to their inherent electron transparency, enabling atomic-resolution imaging without FIB lamella preparation and associated ion-beam damage. A novel micro-shuttle transfer strategy enables controlled placement of a defined number of nanoplates at the reaction site with precise crystallographic orientation. This establishes the foundation for quantitative structure reactivity correlation by enabling simultaneous, spatially resolved detection of reaction products and atomic-scale structural dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a Local Probe Mass Spectrometer (LPMS) integrated with aberration-corrected ETEM to overcome limitations of conventional ETEM-MS setups. By removing SiN windows, using local gas sampling via a micro-capillary, and employing electron-transparent Co3O4 nanoplates with micro-shuttle transfer, the system enables simultaneous atomic-resolution imaging and spatially resolved product detection for quantitative structure-reactivity correlation.
AI.motivation: Current ETEM-MS approaches face a trade-off: closed-cell setups degrade spatial resolution due to diffuse scattering from SiN windows, while open-cell configurations dilute reaction products during transport to the mass spectrometer, preventing accurate structure-reactivity correlation.
AI.method: The LPMS integrates a DENSsolution Stream holder with a MS, removes both SiN membranes of the MEMS chip to preserve resolution while maintaining gas environment via the ETEM chamber, samples reaction products locally via a micro-capillary near the catalyst connected to a holder gas line, and uses Co3O4 nanoplates (electron-transparent, avoiding FIB damage) with a micro-shuttle transfer strategy for controlled placement with precise crystallographic orientation.
AI.result: Initial validation in environmental SEM confirmed controlled gas delivery to the MS. The approach enables atomic-resolution imaging of Co3O4 nanoplates without ion-beam damage and allows simultaneous, spatially resolved detection of reaction products alongside atomic-scale structural dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The LPMS-ETEM integration establishes a foundation for quantitative structure-reactivity correlation by overcoming the resolution-sensitivity trade-off, enabling simultaneous atomic-resolution imaging and localized product detection for dynamic catalytic processes.

title: Atomic scale demonstration of ferromagnetism in a single layer FeCl2 on Au(111)
summary: FeCl2 is a promising single-layer material with sizeable magnetic susceptibility and insulating character that can be easily grown by molecular beam epitaxy on various surfaces. In order to include it into the select palette of van der Waals materials used to engineer functional heterostructures, it is necessary to confirm its magnetic and electronic ground states, and understand the influence of the supporting substrate. In this work, we unambiguously demonstrate ferromagnetic ordering in a single-layer FeCl2 on Au(111) by means of spin-polarized scanning tunnelling microscopy. The material features a relatively wide insulating gap of 3.3 eV and a strongly spin-polarized conduction band that emerges at 1.5 eV above the Fermi level. Atomic scale defects with triangular shape play a primary role in the electronic gap and spin density distribution. Specifically, in a region of 1.6 nm around each defect, the conduction band is locally suppressed and the tunnelling magneto-conductance is reduced a factor of four. By tracking the spin-dependent tunnelling conductance as a function of the applied magnetic field, we record atomically resolved hysteresis loops, revealing a soft ferromagnetic ground state with pronounced out-of-plane anisotropy and coercive fields in the range of 15-50 mT.

AI.tldr: This work confirms ferromagnetic ordering in single-layer FeCl2 on Au(111) using spin-polarized STM, revealing a 3.3 eV insulating gap, a spin-polarized conduction band 1.5 eV above EF, and atomic-scale triangular defects that locally suppress conduction and reduce magneto-conductance fourfold. Hysteresis loops show soft ferromagnetism with out-of-plane anisotropy and coercive fields of 15-50 mT.
AI.motivation: To confirm the magnetic and electronic ground states of single-layer FeCl2 and understand the influence of the supporting substrate, enabling its integration into van der Waals heterostructures.
AI.method: Spin-polarized scanning tunnelling microscopy (SP-STM) to probe magnetic ordering, electronic structure, and spin-dependent transport; atomically resolved hysteresis loop measurements as a function of applied magnetic field.
AI.result: Ferromagnetic ordering in single-layer FeCl2 on Au(111); 3.3 eV insulating gap; strongly spin-polarized conduction band at 1.5 eV above EF; triangular atomic-scale defects locally suppress the conduction band and reduce tunnelling magneto-conductance by a factor of 4 over ~1.6 nm; soft ferromagnetic ground state with out-of-plane anisotropy and coercive fields of 15-50 mT.
AI.conclusion: Single-layer FeCl2 on Au(111) is a ferromagnetic insulator with wide gap and strong spin polarization, making it a viable candidate for van der Waals heterostructures, though atomic-scale defects significantly influence local electronic and magnetic properties.
